span: On a cloth from a cemetery or similar material, one should draw an image of either a man or a woman using substances of the elements <note>referring to ritual paints or minerals</note>. One should then imagine that from the complete transformation of the syllable **Hūṃ**, a sharp axe appears in one's own hand. With that, while reciting the syllable **Phaṭ**, one cuts the neck of the object to be accomplished <note>the enemy</note>. At that time, it is said that "the neck of the enemy will be cut." For that very reason, it is stated: "knowing them to be the object to be accomplished," referring to kings and others. The phrase "possessing the nature of an exceptional body, speech, and mind" refers to those endowed with a very beautiful body. "The superior, middle, and inferior" refers to the Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras <note>the four traditional Indian castes</note>. To those, one does not provide benefit because of their unrighteousness. For that very reason, "remaining in great heedlessness" refers to performing wrathful activities. By this application—the application of the axe—it is certain that "they will be reduced to the fifth state" <note>a euphemism for death</note>. Regarding the phrase "the union of the nectar hearth" and so forth, during a time of heavy rain, one who dwells in the meditative absorption of **Amṛtakuṇḍalin** <gloss>The Swirling Nectar</gloss> should imagine a yellow crossed-vajra <term>viśvavajra</term> arisen from the syllable **Hūṃ** in the direction of the sky over a village or city. In its center, one imagines a blazing vajra arisen from the syllable **Hūṃ**. If one meditates that the rain is dried up by the masses of flames arising from that, it is shown that "the rain will be halted." The phrase "the great mandala of the Vajra Realm" <term>Vajradhātu-mahāmaṇḍala</term> and so forth refers to the time of drawing the great mandala when wind, rain, lightning, and so forth arise from the sky, or when water, snakes, and so forth emerge from beneath the mandala. The word "and so forth" includes earthquakes and the appearance of flesh-eating demons <term>piśāca</term>. "Applied by others" refers to obstacles created by non-Buddhists such as **Gaṇapati** and others. Whenever these occur, at that time, from the complete transformation of the Lord **Amitābha**, one imagines oneself as the noble **Hayagrīva**, with three faces, six arms, and three eyes, standing in the posture with the left leg extended

—tery and substances from the elements to draw the likeness of either a man or a woman. Imagine a sharp axe in one's own hand, transformed from the syllable <term>HUM</term>. By uttering the syllable <term>PHAT</term>, imagine cutting the neck of the target; at that moment, the enemy's neck will be cut. For that very reason, it says "knowing them as the ones to be practiced upon," which refers to kings and others. 

"Possessed of an extraordinary body, speech, and mind" refers to one having a very beautiful body. "Superior, middling, and inferior" refers to the <term>Brahmin</term>, <term>Kshatriya</term>, <term>Vaishya</term>, and <term>Shudra</term> <gloss>the four traditional social classes</gloss>. Because of their unrighteousness, they do not benefit others. For that very reason, "abiding in great heedlessness" refers to those who perform fierce actions. "By this application," specifically the application of the axe, "they will without a doubt become the fifth" <note>an idiom meaning they will die, as the body returns to the four elements</note>.

Regarding "the nectar fire-offering" and so forth: during a time of extreme rainfall, while abiding in the <term>samādhi</term> of <term>Amritakundali</term> <gloss>The Swirling Nectar</gloss>, imagine in the direction of the sky above a village or city a yellow crossed-vajra born from the syllable <term>HUM</term>. In its center, imagine a blazing vajra arising from <term>HUM</term>. It is shown that if one meditates that the mass of flames arising from it dries up the rain, "the rain will be arrested." 

Regarding "the great mandala of the Vajra Realm" and so forth: this refers to the time of drawing the great <term>mandala</term> when wind, rain, and lightning arise from the sky, or when water and snakes and so forth emerge from beneath the mandala. The "and so forth" includes earthquakes and the appearance of <term>pishachas</term> <gloss>flesh-eating spirits</gloss>.
